case.case_title: Kumaranatunga v. Samarasinghe, Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Defence and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 121/82, decided on 3 February 1983

clause.text: Any accused person has the right to a fair trial and legal representation.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner detained under Emergency Regulations had a fundamental right to legal representation during detention.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that conditions of detention preventing correspondence and communication violated his fundamental right to legal representation under Article 13(3).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that Article 13(3) and Section 260 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apply only to persons accused in court, not to persons detained preventively under Emergency Regulations.
key_facts: Detention order 'B' imposed conditions restricting visits and correspondence.
Petitioner was detained preventively under Regulation 17 of Emergency Regulations.
Article 13(3) guarantees legal representation at a fair trial by a competent court.
Section 260 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides right to legal representation for accused persons in court.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 13(3) protects the right to legal representation for persons charged and tried in court, not for persons held under preventive detention orders. Preventive detention is executive, not judicial, and thus does not confer the right to legal representation until the matter is brought before a court.
reasoning.application_to_facts: Since the petitioner was detained preventively and not charged or tried in court, the restrictions on correspondence and visits did not violate Article 13(3). The court noted that as a matter of practice, courts have allowed lawyer visits to detainees to enable representations against detention validity, but no fundamental right to legal representation exists during preventive detention.
principles_established: Article 13(3) right to legal representation applies only to accused persons in court proceedings.
Preventive detention under Emergency Regulations is an executive action, not a judicial process.
No fundamental right to legal representation exists during preventive detention until court proceedings commence.

outcome.holding: The court held that there is no fundamental right to legal representation for persons detained under Regulation 17 of the Emergency Regulations until the matter is brought to court.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(3) was directly considered in relation to the petitioner's claim about legal representation rights during preventive detention, and the court clarified its limited application.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court stated that Article 13(3) and Section 260 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apply to persons accused in court, not to those held on preventive detention orders, and thus no fundamental right to legal representation exists during such detention.
